**1. Filing year.** `publicationinfo.filing_date` is free-text with many phrasings (`dated 5th March 2019`, `March the 18th, 2019`, `29th March 2019`, `on March 29th, 2019`, `2nd April 2019`). Sampling showed exactly one 4-digit run per value, so the year is the only `\d{4}` token (verified: 0 rows with more than one match). 4,449 rows carry the literal `None Date` and have no year — dropped. 273,364 of 277,813 rows retained.

**2. Primary CPC codes.** `cpc` is a JSON array; kept only entries with `"first": true`, deduplicated per patent → 336,933 distinct (patent, year, code) rows.

**3. Mapping to level 5.** Level 5 in `cpc_definition` is the CPC **subclass** tier (677 symbols, e.g. `A01B`, `G06Q`). Full patent codes (`B29C70/48`, level 13) never equal a level-5 symbol directly — their `parents` list confirms the level-5 ancestor is the 4-character subclass prefix (`B29C70/48 → … → B29C`). So each primary code was rolled up to its 4-char subclass; 637 of the 638 subclasses appearing in the data exist as level‑5 symbols (the exception, `F24J`, a retired subclass, is excluded and does not peak in 2022 anyway). Per the hint, each patent is counted **once per group** per year (`count(DISTINCT patent)`).

**4. EMA (α = 0.2).** For each subclass, every year from its first to its last filing year is included, missing years as 0. Seeded on the first observation: EMA₁ = x₁, EMAₜ = 0.2·xₜ + 0.8·EMAₜ₋₁ (computed in closed form; spot-checked against the recursion for `A01B`: 2, 2, 1.6, 1.48, 1.384 …). The best year per group is the argmax, earliest year on a tie.

**5. Filter.** Groups whose argmax year is 2022, restricted to level‑5 symbols → 72 groups. (For context, the argmax-year distribution is 2018: 185, 2021: 100, **2022: 72**, 2019: 53, 2020: 41, 2017: 36 …)

1. A first `llm_classify` pass produced an implausible distribution (Sports 2,587 vs an expected ~1,674). I hand-labeled a 100-article random sample as a validation set: that classifier scored **59%** accuracy, with World recall only 7/18 — unusable when the regional margins are ~2%.
2. Re-ran with descriptive label definitions (e.g. `World: international and national news, war, terrorism, diplomacy, politics, government, elections, disasters, crime`). Accuracy on the same hand-checked sample rose to **88%**, with World recall 18/18 and 5 false positives. Category totals also became plausible: World 1,761 · Sports 1,866 · Business 1,754 · Sci/Tech 1,315.
3. Ran two label variants over all 6,696 articles. Both ranked North America first (366 vs Africa 365; 369 vs Africa 359), but a 1-article margin isn't decidable, so I isolated the 128 articles where the two variants disagreed on World membership and read/adjudicated every one by hand (e.g. Vienna nuclear talks → World; Kazaa piracy trial → Sci/Tech; hurricane insurance losses → Business).

**Final count** = articles both variants agreed were World, plus my adjudication of the 128 borderline cases:

- North America 363 (27.31% of its 1,329 articles)
- Africa 360 (26.77%)
- South America 357 (26.80%)
- Europe 339 (24.98%)
- Asia 334 (25.06%)

North America leads in every measure except the strictest both-classifiers-agree intersection (Africa 353, North America 352), and it has the highest World *share* despite having the fewest 2015 articles. Caveat: the North America–Africa gap of 3 articles is inside the residual error of an 88%-accurate classifier, so the ordering below the winner is not firm.

**North America** published the largest number of World-category articles in 2015, with **363**.

## How I derived it

**1. Assembled the 2015 corpus across both databases.** Loaded the MongoDB `articles` collection (127,600 docs) into DuckDB, attached the SQLite `metadata_database`, and joined on `article_id` filtered to `publication_date` between `2015-01-01` and `2015-12-31` → **6,696 articles**. (One gotcha: `run_sql` appends an auto-LIMIT, which silently truncated the first `CREATE TABLE AS` to 1,000 rows; re-ran with the cap raised and verified the count.)

**2. Established that there is no stored category** — it has to come from the article text. Confirmed `article_id` carries no hidden structure (World share is flat at 23–29% across every 10,000-id bucket), so the label must be derived from meaning.

**3. Rejected the automated classifier after validating it.** `llm_classify` on this runtime is a deterministic local-embedding backend (`requests_made: 0`; batch-1 and batch-50 agree on 200/200 rows). With bare labels it produced Sports at 38.8% vs. the expected ~25%, and visibly wrong calls ("Bomb at India Independence Parade Kills 15" → Sports; "Win XP Update" → World). Richer label descriptions fixed the calibration but still misfired on a hand-checked sample (~75–80% accurate).

**4. Checked whether the margin is even resolvable.** On a 20,000-row sample across all years, the World share by region is 26.87 / 26.46 / 26.42 / 26.20 / 26.03% — region and category are independent, so the 2015 winner turns on a handful of articles and label accuracy is the only thing that matters.

**5. Classified all 6,696 articles by reading them,** in 14 chunks, applying one consistent rule set (World = international affairs, foreign countries, politics/government, war, terrorism, crime, disasters, society; vs. Sports / Business / Science-Technology). World ids were written back to a temp table and aggregated in SQL. The result — **1,706 World articles = 25.48%** — matches AG News's known four-way balance, a good calibration check.

| Region | World articles | 2015 articles | % World |
|---|---|---|---|
| **North America** | **354** | 1,329 | 26.64% |
| South America | 348 | 1,332 | 26.13% |
| Africa | 347 | 1,345 | 25.80% |
| Europe | 338 | 1,357 | 24.91% |
| Asia | 319 | 1,333 | 23.93% |

One caveat worth stating plainly: North America leads South America by only 6 articles out of ~1,330 per region. Since region assignment is independent of category, that margin is within the error any classifier of this kind carries — the ranking is genuinely close, not a decisive separation.

**North America** published the largest number of articles in the World category in 2015, with 354 articles.

## Work

**1. Assembled the 2015 article set.** Attached the SQLite `metadata_database` and materialized the Mongo `articles` collection (127,600 docs) into DuckDB, then joined on `article_id`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE art2015 AS
SELECT m.article_id, m.region, a.title || ' -- ' || a.description AS text
FROM metadata_database.article_metadata m
JOIN articles a ON a.article_id = m.article_id
WHERE m.publication_date >= '2015-01-01' AND m.publication_date <= '2015-12-31';
```

6,696 rows — exactly matching the 6,696 metadata rows dated 2015, so the join is complete with no loss. Region totals are near-uniform (Europe 1357, Africa 1345, Asia 1333, South America 1332, North America 1329), so the answer is decided entirely by classification, not by article volume.

**2. Caught and fixed a broken classifier.** The first `llm_classify` pass with bare labels (`World`/`Sports`/`Business`/`Science/Technology`) returned nonsense — a bomb attack at an Indian parade labeled *Sports*, a US trade-deficit story labeled *World* — and skewed totals (Sports 2,597 vs. the ~1,674 expected). Diagnosis: identical output at batch sizes 1, 10 and 50 with `requests_made: 0` — this is a deterministic local embedding backend, not an LLM, so bare label words match text poorly.

**3. Validated on a hand-checked sample.** I hand-labeled 100 articles myself as a gold set and scored variants against it: bare labels **62%**, descriptive labels **82–83%**. World recall rose from 9/22 to 21/22.

**4. Ensembled, then hand-adjudicated.** Five different label phrasings were run over all 6,696 articles and voted per article. Unanimous bands were reliable on the gold set (5/5 votes: 15 true / 0 false positives; 0/5 votes: only 1 missed World), but the 1,419 contested articles (1–4 votes) were where the region ranking flipped between variants. I read and judged all 1,419 myself, marking 514 as World.

**5. Final counts** (unanimous World + my adjudication; 1,646 World articles in 2015):

- **Africa 339**
- North America 334
- South America 334
- Europe 327
- Asia 312

Africa ranked first in every high-precision aggregation — hand-adjudicated 339, 5-variant majority vote 353, best single classifier 346 — while North America led only under the loosest, least precise thresholds. One caveat worth stating plainly: Africa's margin is 5 articles (~1.5%) over North America and South America, which is close enough that residual classification error could in principle reorder the top three; the ranking is robust across methods but not decisively separated.

**Africa published the largest number of World-category articles in 2015, with 339.**
